narrative:
The model determined that you have a 30% chance of representing a bad credit risk. Because this probability crossed the threshold the bank uses for approval, your loan application was denied.

Three pieces of information about you weighed most heavily in that decision. First, the length of the loan you requested had the strongest influence overall. At only 9 months it was much shorter than the 19-month average among approved applicants; while this shorter duration actually pushed the prediction slightly toward approval, the model still saw enough risk elsewhere to deny the request. 

The second most important factor was the status of your checking account. You currently have a negative balance, a situation that appears in only 12.6% of approved applicants. This feature pushed the prediction strongly toward bad credit risk.

Third, your employment duration of 4–7 years also mattered. This length of stable work is somewhat less common than the longest-tenured or very recently hired groups among approved customers, and it nudged the prediction slightly toward higher risk.

Taken together, the negative checking-account status and your employment situation outweighed the positive signal from the short loan duration, leading to the denial.

You should focus on two practical next steps: bring your checking account balance above zero and, if possible, wait until you have been with your employer for at least seven years before re-applying. These changes would directly address the two factors that most hurt your application.
